preheader: Graeber on bureaucracy as a way of organising stupidity; block an unattended agent from writing outside its working directories; Binance lost about $6.3 billion from a hot wallet after a DevOps laptop was compromised; a backdoored Claude Code extension on the Cursor marketplace opened a reverse SSH tunnel; thirteen House Democrats want a vote on refusing to bail out AI firms; Martin Fowler says do not let an LLM write your first draft; a gist says 16% of one user's Claude Code spend went on status-line summaries; Claude found seven documentation defects eleven human reviewers missed; markets were shut on Saturday, so Friday: Sensex 74,459.53 (+308.49) and Nifty 23,053.10 (+116.35) on 681 advances against 2,097 declines; the Centre has spent 42.1% of its full-year deficit in six months; Google Play now forbids apps from deceiving AI agents; a cupboard in Pompeii held a child's rattling amulets and 38 bronze coins; your yellow pencil is a 137-year-old advertisement.

quote.text: Bureaucracies, I've suggested, are not themselves forms of stupidity so much as they are ways of organizing stupidity
quote.author: David Graeber
quote.work: The Utopia of Rules: On Technology, Stupidity, and the Secret Joys of Bureaucracy
quote.note: The ordinary complaint is that bureaucracies are stupid, which locates the fault in the people inside them and is therefore comforting: replace them and the problem goes. Graeber moves the fault into the architecture. The form does not contain stupidity, it distributes it — each person holds a piece too small to be wrong about, and the stupidity lives in the joins where nobody is standing. Which is why the clever, decent, well-meaning staff of an organisation can reliably produce an outcome not one of them would have chosen, and why nobody can tell you who decided it.

items.text: If you run Claude Code unattended — bypass mode, a cron job, a CI step — turn on `permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories`. Since 2.1.314 it makes Write, Edit and NotebookEdit refuse any path outside your working directories in every permission mode, so a session that goes wrong can still only go wrong inside the repo. Bypass mode skips the prompt; this setting is the floor underneath it.

hn.title: Binance-hacker-1029 – $5.6B stolen from Binance
bullets: The linked page is an Arkham Intelligence entity tracker and will not serve to a fetch, so these bullets come from CoinDesk's and BleepingComputer's 29-30 October accounts. Treat the headline's $5.6B as a snapshot that has since moved: Arkham's label 'binance-hacker-1029' describes the balance held across the attacker's addresses, not a settled loss. BleepingComputer counted 55 addresses holding about $5.78 billion; later tallies put the entity at 66 addresses and $5.88 billion. Binance's own figure for the impact is about $6.3 billion. Chainalysis estimated $5.9 billion at the moment of the theft.

The mechanism, per Binance's preliminary finding, was not cryptography. A DevOps engineer's laptop was compromised, which gave the attacker a path into a service container from which unauthorised withdrawals could be submitted. Binance says it has found no evidence of a wallet private key leak. For scale, DefiLlama put Binance's pre-hack holdings at about $144 billion, so roughly 4% of the exchange walked out through an endpoint.

Stablecoins are the part of the stack that can be reversed, and they were. Tether froze more than $1.567 billion in USDT and Circle more than $800 million in USDC — over $2.3 billion between them, out of about $3 billion Binance says was frozen in total. The attacker also pushed funds through Uniswap and borrowed at least 20,000 WETH, about $44 million, from Aave against stolen USDT, which is what you do when the tokens you hold are the freezable ones.

Prices moved the way they do: bitcoin −4.8% to below $77,000, ether −5.7%, BNB −8%, AAVE −11%. Binance suspended withdrawals and said it would cover losses from the SAFU fund and company money; co-CEO Yi He said it would cover all of them. TRM Labs attributed the attack to the North Korean group TraderTraitor with high confidence; ZachXBT and Blockaid also pointed at North Korea. Comparison worth keeping: the Bybit heist in February 2025, the largest confirmed crypto theft until this week, was $1.5 billion.

hn.title: Backdoor in Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace
bullets: Version 2.1.313 of the Claude Code extension, as published on the Cursor marketplace, shipped with a prefix injected into `extension.js`. It runs when Node loads the file — before `activate` — so installing is enough. Cursor pulled the release, and the 2.1.313 versions were pulled from the NPM and VS Code registries too. Phorion's advisory, by Calum Hall, is dated 30 October.

What it installs is plain old SSH persistence rather than anything clever. It appends an attacker's Ed25519 public key to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` with the comment `svc-telemetry`, then dials out to 134.209.82.225 on port 22 as user `tunnel` with an embedded private key and requests `-R *:0:localhost:22` — a reverse forward, so the operator reaches your sshd through a port the server picks. It retries every 60 seconds and keeps running after the editor closes.

Persistence is per-platform and sloppy: a user LaunchAgent on macOS named `com.apple.sysmond.plist` pointing at `~/.config/.smt`, a crontab `@reboot` entry on Linux, a `SysMon` scheduled task or Startup-folder script on Windows. Phorion notes the macOS Remote Login check and the Windows enablement path both have bugs, so on those platforms the keys and persistence often land while SSH itself does not get switched on.

The beacon is the detail worth copying into your own threat model. One plaintext HTTP POST to 134.209.82.225:8099/beacon carries hostname, username, OS, architecture, home and working directories, your global Git email, your public IP from ifconfig.me or api.ipify.org — and the *names*, not the values, of environment variables matching `KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP`. A list of which secrets you hold is a targeting document even when the secrets stay home.

hn.title: US Reps Lead Democratic Resolution Opposing A.I. Bubble Bailout for Big Tech
bullets: Introduced 29 October by Greg Casar (TX-35), who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus, and Maxine Waters (CA-43), ranking member on House Financial Services. Eleven others signed on — Danny Davis, Chris Deluzio, Valerie Foushee, Jesús 'Chuy' García, Pramila Jayapal, Analilia Mejia, Delia Ramirez, André Carson, Jan Schakowsky, Brad Sherman and Rashida Tlaib — making thirteen names on a non-binding sense-of-the-House resolution.

The specific things it asks the federal government to refuse are narrower than 'no bailout': emergency lending or direct capital infusions that keep an insolvent AI firm out of ordinary bankruptcy, and golden parachutes for executives whose risky or illegal conduct caused the insolvency. It asks instead for full legal accountability and the return of ill-gotten assets, and it names them — luxury homes, yachts, private planes.

The economic claim is about where the debt sits. The resolution says AI-related firms hold trillions of dollars in debt, much of it raised in opaque, unregulated private credit markets, and that the market's price-to-earnings ratio is nearly as high as at the peak of the 1990s tech bubble. Its 2008 comparison is specific too: trillions in liquidity to the financial sector, about 10 million homeowners losing their homes, tens of millions of workers without adequate employment for years.

It is a marker, not a law — and Casar has said as much, wanting a vote early in the next Congress if not sooner, so that members are on the record before there is anything to vote on. The asks on the other side of the ledger are the ordinary countercyclical list: direct job spending, support for state and local services, unemployment insurance, nutrition and housing aid, protection for pension holders, and automatic stabilisers that fire when a downturn starts rather than when Congress agrees it has.

hn.title: LLM Voice
bullets: Fowler's 29 October entry names a thing readers already react to and writers mostly deny: 'LLM Voice', the quality that makes prose feel generated. His diagnosis is not the em-dash, which he explicitly clears. It is over-polish — his example of the tell is the phrase 'load-bearing tapestries' — and he calls the reaction an 'uncanny valley of prose'. By the time a detector flags the text, he argues, the damage is already done, because the reader felt it on the first paragraph.

The advice is unusually absolute for him: do not have an LLM write a draft, and be wary of accepting its rephrasings. An outline, maybe. His stated reason is not aesthetic but cognitive — writing is a way of thinking, so handing off the writing hands off some of the thinking. He uses AI as a search tool only, verifies anything it surfaces at the source, and asks that anyone using AI to write disclose how, usually in the acknowledgements.

He then argues against himself, which is the part worth reading. He doubts his own ability to detect LLM Voice; some phrases he dislikes ('sales motion', 'sharp round-up') turn out to be used by humans, so the difference he is sensing may be generational rather than mechanical. He knows of one fully LLM-drafted piece with no LLM Voice in it — it took a professional editor to get there. And he finds the prospect of the tell disappearing altogether more worrying than the tell.

The exceptions he allows are specific people rather than categories: Jim Highsmith, using an LLM to keep writing with Parkinson's disease; colleagues writing in a second language, whose clunky human prose he says he prefers to smooth machine prose; and form letters nobody will read. Nine people commented on his drafts, and he states plainly that no AI was used to write the post.

hn.title: Claude Code regularly sends each background agent's transcript to its model
bullets: The claim, from the Flamerix AI account: roughly every 30 seconds Claude Code re-sends each background agent's full transcript to a model, and the output is used only to write that agent's three-to-five-word status line. The gist says this has been on by default since 2.1.232, with no setting to turn it off, and ships a Bun preload hook (`no-agent-summary.js`, MIT) that suppresses it.

Separate the demonstrated from the extrapolated. Demonstrated: version-by-version counts of summary forks on Linux, mostly 5 with no hook, 5 with the hook in `pass` mode and 0 in `off` mode, with bundle anchor strings and sha256 checksums published so you can rerun it — and several commenters reproducing 5/5/0 on macOS and Windows. Extrapolated: the headline '15-20% of tokens'.

That percentage rests on one user's OpenTelemetry data, grouped by `query_source = agent_summary`: 16.4% of spend and 19.7% of requests before the hook, zero after. The author is careful that 'spend' is Claude Code's own per-request estimate rather than an invoice, and that the share is workload-specific. A linked issue reports four measurements in the 18-26% range. So the mechanism is well evidenced; the number is one data point with a shape.

Two open threads. The commenter wtfsayo argues the gist's claim that summaries never reach the model is wrong, reporting summary text reappearing in later context through stored progress data — unresolved. And the explanation for why no off switch exists is inferred from the bundled code, not stated by Anthropic. Windows suppression in a live session, the desktop app and the ACP/SDK paths are untested.

stories.headline: Both benchmarks closed up and three stocks fell for every one that rose — Friday was two sectors and a stronger rupee doing the work
stories.source: Liquide's 30 October closing report for the index levels, sector moves, Bank Nifty and the movers; Trendlyne's Marketwatch for the closing breadth, the Nifty 500 and India VIX; Kotak Neo's NSE FII/DII table for the cash flows; PTI via Telangana Today for the rupee and the dollar index
bullets: Friday 30 October: Sensex 74,459.53, up 308.49 points or 0.42%; Nifty 50 23,053.10, up 116.35 or 0.51%. Nifty IT rose 2.32% and Pharma 1.55%. Every other sector index fell. Bank Nifty was down 0.41%. An index can rise on two sectors when those two are heavy enough, and that is the whole of Friday.

The breadth number is the one to keep. 681 stocks advanced against 2,097 that declined, out of 2,842 traded — and the Nifty 500 actually fell 0.22%. If you held the index you had a good day; if you held a basket you probably did not. India VIX ticking up 2.3% to 15.5 on a rising day fits that picture rather than contradicting it.

Institutional flows inverted from Thursday exactly. FIIs bought a net ₹3,598.54 crore in the cash market after selling ₹943.60 crore the session before; DIIs sold ₹817.51 crore after buying ₹1,924.41 crore. Two sessions, two reversals. Provisional daily cash flows are a record of what happened, not a signal about what comes next, and this week is a good argument for reading them that way.

The rupee gained 33 paise to 94.93, its first look under 95 in a while, helped by a dollar index down 0.37% to 101.66. That is a decent chunk of why foreign money came back in on the same day. Note that nothing here describes today: Saturday is not a trading session, and the next close is Monday's.

trends.headline: Six months into the year the Centre has already run 42.1% of its full-year deficit, and the gap is a quarter wider than last year's
trends.subject: Union deficit for April to September stood at 7.15 trillion rupees against 5.70 trillion a year before, with net tax revenue rising just 4 per cent to 12.8 trillion while spending rose 11 per cent to 25.5 trillion and capex hit 6.5 trillion, so 42.1 per cent of the 16.96 trillion annual ceiling is already used.
trends.subtitle: Reuters via Business Recorder, on the government data released Friday 30 October 2026
bullets: ₹7.15 lakh crore ($75.24 billion) of deficit in the first half, against ₹5.7 lakh crore a year earlier — about 25% more. Measured against the full-year target of ₹16.96 lakh crore, or 4.3% of GDP, that is 42.1% used in six months. Half a year, two-fifths of the budget: on its own that is not alarming, because Indian government spending is front-loaded and receipts arrive late. The composition is more interesting than the headline.

Revenue is growing slowly. Net tax receipts came to ₹12.8 lakh crore against ₹12.3 lakh crore a year ago — roughly 4% more in nominal terms, which after inflation is close to flat. Non-tax revenue barely moved, ₹4.8 lakh crore against ₹4.7 lakh crore. This is the first full year of the restructured GST rates, and a tax base that grows 4% nominally is the number to watch rather than the deficit ratio.

Spending is growing much faster. Total expenditure was ₹25.5 lakh crore against ₹23 lakh crore, about 11% up. Capital expenditure — roads, rail, the physical stuff — rose from ₹5.8 to ₹6.5 lakh crore, and so accounts for roughly ₹0.7 lakh crore of the ₹2.5 lakh crore increase. The remaining ₹1.8 lakh crore is revenue spending, and Reuters attributes a good part of it to a spike in food and fertiliser subsidies.

The arithmetic for the second half is therefore tight but not unusual: ₹9.8 lakh crore of room left, against a half-year in which the deficit ran at ₹1.19 lakh crore a month. Receipts do pick up — advance tax, dividends, the RBI transfer — and the target is usually met or nearly met. The thing that would change that is the subsidy line, not the capex line.

trends.headline: Google Play now forbids an app from deceiving an AI agent, which is a rule written to protect the software rather than the user
trends.subject: Google Play's 29 October 2026 policy announcement adds an AppFunctions API policy stating apps are strictly prohibited from deceiving or manipulating AI agents, with at least 30 days to comply.
trends.subtitle: Google Play's developer policy announcement of 29 October 2026, in Play Console Help
bullets: The new AppFunctions API policy is three clauses long. Developers must follow all existing Play policies; apps are 'strictly prohibited from deceiving or manipulating AI agents'; and they may not bypass security controls or interfere with other applications. Developers get at least 30 days from 29 October to comply. AppFunctions is the surface through which an on-device agent calls into an installed app, so this is the rule for the moment the agent becomes the customer.

It is worth noticing what kind of rule it is. Store policy has always protected the user from the app and the platform from the app. This protects a piece of software from the app — the agent is now a party that can be lied to, with standing. Everything an app currently does to a human to win attention or a tap becomes, pointed at an agent, a policy violation. Separately, the same announcement clarifies that developers 'cannot engage in behaviors that manipulate the app review process', which is the older version of the same worry.

The other agentic item in the announcement is quieter and probably bigger: Google says it is giving additional guidance on how the Payments policy applies to apps that facilitate digital purchases through AI or agentic experiences. The announcement does not state the requirements, only that the guidance exists — so the question of who owes Play its cut when an agent, not a person, completes the purchase is being answered somewhere other than in the policy summary.

The rest of the 29 October list is permission-tightening of the ordinary kind, and the dates matter if you ship Android. Local Network and Manage Contacts permissions are now restricted to core functionality with a Play Console declaration for apps targeting API 37 (Android 17). From 27 January 2027 location scope is mandated, the Android location button is required for one-time requests, and phone-call verification stops being a permitted use of READ_CALL_LOG. Trader status must be declared in Play Console from November 2026, and Japan payments authorisation is due by 1 December or payouts are held globally.

trends.headline: A cupboard in Pompeii was opened after 1,947 years and the most valuable thing in it was a child's rattle
trends.subject: Excavation of a household cupboard in a house on Via dell'Abbondanza at Pompeii, announced by the Pompeii Archaeological Park on 29 October 2026, containing a necklace of at least 24 crepundia amulets, 38 bronze coins in a woven container, toiletry items and lead trading weights.
trends.subtitle: Archaeology Magazine's 30 October report, on the Pompeii Archaeological Park's announcement and Gabriel Zuchtriegel's comments
bullets: The house is on Via dell'Abbondanza, central Pompeii, and inscriptions — no longer visible, so the attribution is soft — point to a Cornelius Maximus. Inside the cupboard: a necklace of at least 24 crepundia, amulets in bone, glass paste, earthenware and rock crystal. Some carry images of Bes and Mercury. Others are small hands, feet, pinecones and bunches of grapes.

Crepundia were worn by children, and they were not only charms. They rattled. The protective function and the practical one are the same object: a parent in a crowded street could hear where the child was. That is the detail that collapses nineteen centuries — the problem being solved is the one every parent in a market still has.

Alongside it, the ordinary inventory of a household: tweezers, a small glass bottle for perfume or ointment, an incense burner, a cooking pot, vessels in bronze, glass and ceramic, and lead weights in a wooden box, which suggests somebody in the house traded. And a small woven container holding 38 bronze coins — the household's loose change, left where it was.

The park's director Gabriel Zuchtriegel is careful about what it proves: the occupant cannot be reconstructed with certainty, and the value of the find is that the fragments bring researchers 'closer to their daily life'. Which is the argument for digging up cupboards rather than villas. One caveat the coverage raises: other recent Pompeii excavations have found traces of people who came back afterwards to dig for their belongings, so 'sealed since AD 79' is an inference about this cupboard, not a finding.

research.title: Claude read 1,061 pages of manufacturing and regulatory documentation, found all eleven problems the human reviewers found, and seven they had missed
research.subject: Anthropic life-sciences partnerships with six drug developers: Enveda had Claude review 1,061 pages of manufacturing and regulatory documentation, catching all 11 issues human reviewers found plus seven they missed and cutting human review from over 25 hours to under three; BigHat tested about 1,010 antibody-fragment variants in ten weeks.
research.subtitle: Anthropic, 'Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude', 27 October 2026
bullets: The interesting half of this write-up is not the molecule design, which is where everyone looks. It is Enveda, where Claude was pointed at 1,061 pages of manufacturing and regulatory documentation. It caught all 11 issues the human reviewers had found and seven they had not. Human review time fell 89%, from over 25 hours to under three. It also drafted two regulatory documents: one took four hours against roughly three months by hand, and human review of the draft found a single minor error.

That is a different claim from 'AI designs drugs'. The binding constraint on a small drug developer is rarely chemistry — it is the volume of paperwork that stands between a result and permission to use it, and paperwork is the one part of the pipeline where a language model is working in its native material. The lab results are the ones that need wet-lab confirmation; this one needs a regulator.

The lab numbers are real but small-n and preclinical. At Generate Biomedicines six scientists used Claude Code to redesign a genetic component of a CAR T-cell therapy; one design came out about 70% shorter than standard and let immune cells make roughly 10 times as many cancer-spotting receptors. Divergence Labs generated about 35,000 antibody designs in a month against food allergy, yielding three that bind IgE and 20 that dislodge it, three of those better than the standard medication. BigHat's lab tested about 1,010 antibody-fragment variants over ten weeks; the best bound more than 10 times more tightly, one stayed in solution 18°C higher, another clumped more than 100 times more slowly.

Read the structure of the post as carefully as the results. Anthropic has acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person rare-muscular-dystrophy company whose founder used Claude to coordinate 11 external labs, and says a candidate went from idea to promising mouse results in under 18 months, with human trials possibly in late 2028. Bristol Myers Squibb is using it to score early clinical trial plans. None of this has been in a human yet, every figure is the company's own, and the BigHat result explicitly needed human scientists to refine and run the revised protocol.

research.title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
research.subject: SmoothScore grades each conclusive assertion in an agent-written synthesis against retrieved evidence on a one-to-five scale; across 7 systems and 4 benchmarks no pairing fell below 22 per cent materially overstated assertions, with Gemini Deep Research at 22-35 per cent severe and GPT Luna 5.6 at 1-4 per cent.
research.subtitle: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa and Greg Durrett, New York University, arXiv:2610.35793, 26 October 2026
bullets: The failure they name is 'smoothing'. A research agent reads a corpus in which sources disagree, and writes one confident narrative. Nothing in the report is a fabricated citation — the citations are real and the claims are stronger than they support, because the disagreement in the corpus got averaged away. It is a hallucination of certainty rather than of fact, which is why it survives the checks everyone currently runs.

SmoothScore works claim by claim: pull the conclusive claims out of a generated report, retrieve the evidence for each, cluster that evidence by high-level aspect, then score the claim against it on a 1-5 scale. The judge lands within one point of a human annotator on 93% of claims. Code and data are at github.com/tiasa2/SmoothScore.

Across 7 systems and 4 datasets — ResearcherBench, ScholarQA-CS2, DeepResearch Bench II, ResearchRubrics — every single system-dataset pair had at least 22% of claims at 3 or above, the threshold they treat as materially smoothed, and for most systems it was over half. Mean scores: GPT Luna 5.6 1.66-1.95 and GPT Sol 5.6 1.82-1.93 at the good end, most systems 2.20-2.88, Gemini Deep Research 3.05-3.27. At severe smoothing (4+), Luna and Sol sit at 1-4% of claims; Gemini at 22-35%.

The open-weights systems do not sort the way the argument usually goes. DR Tulu and QUEST score at or slightly above Claude Sonnet 5, with 55-59% of claims at 3+ and 7-23% at 4+. Two closed systems are the least smoothed and one closed system is the most. Whatever controls this is a training and decoding choice rather than a property of being open or closed — which is the encouraging reading, because it means it is fixable.

wild.headline: Karwa Chauth is observed by looking at the moon through a sieve, so a bag brand built a fifteen-foot sieve and hung it over the road
wild.subject: Zouk ran a 40-foot outdoor billboard carrying a 15-foot three-dimensional channi for Karwa Chauth 2026 with Laqshya Media, tagline 'Pati's who gift Zouk, stay sukh'.
wild.subtitle: Adgully's 29 October write-up of the activation, with the agency and tagline as stated there
bullets: The channi is the sieve a woman looks through to see the moon before breaking the Karwa Chauth fast — a small domestic object, held at arm's length, used once a year. Zouk had a 15-foot version built in three dimensions and mounted on a 40-foot billboard, so the thing you are meant to peer through is now the thing you drive under. The outdoor partner was Laqshya Media.

What makes it work as an ad is that the prop needs no caption to anyone who observes the festival, and is meaningless to anyone who does not. That is an unusual bet for a billboard, which is normally built for the lowest common denominator of passing traffic. The copy is a Hinglish pun — 'Pati's who gift Zouk, stay sukh' — and it is aimed squarely at husbands who have not yet bought anything.

Founder Disha Singh frames it as being about the small gestures: 'Festivals like Karwa Chauth celebrate love, traditions and the little gestures that make relationships special.' Zouk, for its part, is a vegan leather-goods brand, so a festival built on a handheld household object is better-matched territory than it first looks. Adgully's report does not give the billboard's location or how long it ran, and some coverage frames the channi as a possible world record, for which there appears to be no category.

wild.headline: A candy brand cut a 22-foot van into a haunted house and built the game Operation into its wall
wild.subject: HI-CHEW's Chewbies Mystery Manor Tour converted a 22-foot van into a mobile haunted house containing a wall-mounted Operation-style game, touring Austin, Nashville, Chicago, Philadelphia and Hoboken in late October 2026.
wild.subtitle: BizBash's 2026 Halloween activation round-up, for the build, the vehicle and the five cities
bullets: The vehicle is the whole idea. Lime Media, working with Inspira Marketing, turned a 22-foot van into what BizBash calls a haunted house on wheels, and the centrepiece inside is an Operation-style game built into the van's wall with the brand mascot Chewbie in the patient's place. You play the wall to retrieve the prize, which is a limited-edition Halloween flavour — green apple, orange creamsicle, cotton candy.

A mobile build is a different economic animal from a pop-up. Five stops — Austin, Nashville, Chicago, Philadelphia and Hoboken, New Jersey — on one fit-out, which is the trade a brand makes when its audience is students who will not travel to an activation but will walk past one. The tour ran through late October, and separate coverage puts the dates at 17-31 October with a $3,000 prize draw and the mystery flavour revealed on Halloween.

There is a neat bit of licensing logic under the oddity, too. Operation is a game about extracting objects from a body cavity without touching the sides — a mechanic that was already about dread rather than skill. Mounting it vertically in a van and swapping the patient for a mascot costs almost nothing in explanation, because every adult who walks up already knows the rules and already knows the buzzer.

wild.headline: A chicken-finger chain's founder grew a 3,156-pound pumpkin, carved witches into it, and held a film premiere for the pumpkin
wild.subject: Raising Cane's founder Todd Graves unveiled a Guinness-certified 3,156-pound jack-o'-lantern at Salem Common on 27 October 2026, grown by Ron Wallace in Green, Rhode Island over 123 days, during Salem's 400th-anniversary year.
wild.subtitle: Boston.com's 28 October local report for the weight, the grower, the carvers and the mayor's proclamation
bullets: 3,156 pounds, certified by Guinness World Records as the heaviest jack-o'-lantern, and per Boston.com the first fruit of any kind past 3,000 pounds. Ron Wallace grew it in Green, Rhode Island over 123 days. It had already taken the heaviest-pumpkin title earlier in the month, before anyone cut into it — so carving it cost one record to set another. Eric Jones, Monique Hawk and William Wilson did the carving, and a photo caption has Graves helping.

What went into it: skeletons, Salem-inspired witches, and the company logo. Salem is in its 400th-anniversary year, and Mayor Dominick Pangallo proclaimed 27 October 'Great Pumpkin Day', with the line 'It's our 400th birthday and we're still out here making history!' Kimberly Brown, who played Marnie Piper in Halloweentown, turned up to say it was the most astounding pumpkin she had ever seen.

The surrounding activity is where it tips into the genuinely odd. A second carved pumpkin, 2,613 pounds, went to Hollywood & Highland in Los Angeles and was given a mock film premiere — 'The Night Of The Raising Cane's', with a faded marquee, tattered directors' chairs and crooked tombstones, per Event Marketer — plus further displays at company offices in Texas and Louisiana. A brand with no seasonal product to sell bought a vegetable, broke a record with it, and then gave it a red carpet.

learn.title: Your pencil is yellow because of a stall at the 1889 Paris exposition, and nobody has repainted it since
learn.subject: Why graphite pencils are conventionally yellow: Hardtmuth of Ceske Budejovice launched the glossy-yellow Koh-i-Noor at the 1889 Exposition Universelle, named for the Crown Jewels diamond, won a Grand Prix for the Koh-i-Noor 1500 at the 1900 Paris Exposition, and competitors copied the colour.
body: There is no reason for a pencil to be yellow. The wood is cedar, which is pinkish. The graphite is grey. The paint does nothing for the writing, adds a step to manufacture, and is the single most recognisable thing about the object. Pick up a pencil anywhere in the world and the odds are good it is the colour of a taxi, and the reason is a trade fair.

In 1889 at the Exposition Universelle in Paris — the one the Eiffel Tower was built for — a small Czech stall showed a pencil made by Hardtmuth of Ceske Budejovice, in Bohemia. The company had patented a lead made by mixing kaolin clay with graphite, which let you control how hard the thing wrote. They put it in a cedar barrel with a glossy yellow finish and named it after the Koh-i-Noor, the diamond that had been set into the British Crown Jewels about forty years earlier. Naming a pencil after the most famous diamond in Europe tells you exactly what the yellow was for. At the next Paris exposition, in 1900, the Koh-i-Noor Hardtmuth 1500 took a Grand Prix, and the yellow barrel became a thing other manufacturers painted their pencils to look like.

The usual next sentence is that yellow signalled Chinese graphite, because the best graphite then came from China and yellow is the imperial colour there. That part is a reconstruction — it is a plausible story told about Hardtmuth rather than one Hardtmuth told about itself, and no company statement of the motive survives. What is documented is the simpler and slightly funnier thing: the colour was a luxury signal that worked, the competition copied the signal rather than the lead, and a hundred and thirty-seven years later you are still holding an advertisement for a pencil most people have never heard of.

items.text: A written-down version of a story they have told you about themselves, handed back to them in your words.
An introduction. Pick two people you know who should know each other, and make the email instead of saying you should.
A voice note for a child, to be opened in twenty years, describing what they were like this month.
items.why: Parents on r/SomebodyMakeThis keep asking for an app that captures small moments before they are forgotten; the hard part was never the app.

items.text: Your afternoon, spent doing the one errand they have been putting off for six months.
A photograph you already have, printed on paper and put in a frame you already own.
Permission. Tell someone plainly that the thing they feel guilty about not doing is fine not to do.
A recommendation with a reason. Not a list of ten books — one book, and two sentences on why it is for them specifically.
An hour of silence in a shared flat: go out, deliberately, so the other person gets the place to themselves.
The thing they lent you, returned. Cleaned.
A compliment delivered to their boss, or their parent, instead of to them.
